verses.text: Hear this word that Yahweh has spoken against you, children of Israel, against the whole family which I brought up out of the land of Egypt, saying:
“I have only chosen you of all the families of the earth. Therefore I will punish you for all of your sins.”
Do two walk together, unless they have agreed?
Will a lion roar in the thicket, when he has no prey? Does a young lion cry out of his den, if he has caught nothing?
Can a bird fall in a trap on the earth, where no snare is set for him? Does a snare spring up from the ground, when there is nothing to catch?
Does the trumpet alarm sound in a city, without the people being afraid? Does evil happen to a city, and Yahweh hasn’t done it?
Surely the Lord Yahweh will do nothing, unless he reveals his secret to his servants the prophets.
The lion has roared. Who will not fear? The Lord Yahweh has spoken. Who can but prophesy?

Proclaim in the palaces at Ashdod, and in the palaces in the land of Egypt, and say, “Assemble yourselves on the mountains of Samaria, and see what unrest is in her, and what oppression is among them.”
“Indeed they don’t know to do right,” says Yahweh, “Who hoard plunder and loot in their palaces.”
Therefore thus says the Lord Yahweh: “An adversary will overrun the land; and he will pull down your strongholds, and your fortresses will be plundered.”

Yahweh says: “As the shepherd rescues out of the mouth of the lion two legs, or a piece of an ear, so shall the children of Israel be rescued who sit in Samaria on the corner of a couch, and on the silken cushions of a bed.”
“Listen, and testify against the house of Jacob,” says the Lord Yahweh, the God of Armies.
“For in the day that I visit the transgressions of Israel on him, I will also visit the altars of Bethel; and the horns of the altar will be cut off, and fall to the ground.
I will strike the winter house with the summer house; and the houses of ivory will perish, and the great houses will have an end,”  says Yahweh.

footnotes.content: Amos speaks as a faithful servant delivering hard news. The Lord's word comes with urgency—not a suggestion, but a message that demands hearing. Notice how Amos reminds Israel that this whole relationship began with rescue: God brought them up out of Egypt with His own hand.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: There's a jaw-clenching honesty here: chosen love and punishment are not enemies. The Lord's choice of Israel makes judgment necessary—He loves too well to stay silent when His people stray into injustice. Grace and accountability travel together.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A simple question that cuts to the bone. How can Israel walk with the Lord while serving idols and wealth? Agreement and companionship require the same direction. The proverb stands as timeless as it is here—two cannot move together unless their hearts align.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The lion roars only when hunting; his cry means consequence is coming. Amos uses images Israel would know from the wilderness: nothing happens without reason. When the Lord speaks, judgment follows—it is not random, not capricious, but as certain as a lion's pounce.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Again, the pattern: a bird does not fall unless the trap is set. A snare does not spring without purpose. Amos teaches Israel that what looks like accident is often consequence—the world runs on order, not chaos. The Lord does not act carelessly.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: This hits hard for those who want to separate God from hard events. The trumpet alarm brings fear; disaster in the city reveals the Lord's hand. Amos refuses false comfort—every consequence flows from the One who holds all things.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The Lord is not hidden; He speaks through His prophets. Before judgment falls, He sends warning. This is mercy beneath the hard word—Amos reminds Israel that the prophets are a gift, that God talks to His people, even in rebuke.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The lion has roared—meaning judgment is set. Now the prophet cannot keep silent; he must speak. Amos is not choosing prophecy for fame or comfort; he is compelled by what he has heard from the Lord. The word burns in him.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Ashdod and Egypt—the pagan neighbors—are called to witness Israel's corruption. The irony stings: Israel, chosen and redeemed, has become a scandal even to the nations around them. Their injustice is so visible that outsiders are invited to see the unrest and oppression festering within.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "They don't know to do right." The Lord's diagnosis is clear: the wealthy hoard plunder in their palaces while the poor cry out. This is not ignorance—it is a forgetting of justice, a turning away from the Lord's heart for the vulnerable.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Now the judgment is named: an adversary will come, strongholds will fall, fortresses will be plundered. The Lord uses the nations as His instrument of justice. Israel's own palaces—built on stolen wealth—will not protect them.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A shepherd rescues fragments—two legs, a piece of an ear—the bare remnants of a lamb already dead. This is what "rescue" will look like for Israel: not victory, but survival of scraps. Those lounging on their couches in Samaria will be stripped even of comfort.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The Lord calls for witnesses—testimony against Jacob, against the whole house. This is a courtroom scene: the case against Israel is being made public, and there is no hiding place.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Bethel—the place where Jacob saw the ladder and the Lord promised blessing—is now the site of false worship. The horns of the altar, where the guilty could flee for mercy, will be cut off. No refuge remains where there is no true allegiance to the true God.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The winter house and summer house, the ivory palaces—all will perish. Readers today hear an echo in the prosperity that crumbles, the luxury that cannot shelter us from the Lord's justice. Only what is built on righteousness stands.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
